Carthusian
kar-THOO-zhun
adj., n. (of the eremitical order founded by Bruno in 1084 at the Grande Chartreuse; a monk of that order)
From Latin Cartusia, the Latin name of the Chartreuse valley in Dauphiné.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Carthusians are the strictest of the western orders and the one that never needed reforming, because it never relaxed. Bruno of Cologne settled six companions in the high valley of Chartreuse in 1084 and built not a dormitory but a row of separate cells around a cloister walk, each with its own garden and workbench. A Carthusian eats alone, works alone, prays most of the office alone, and joins the community only for night office, conventual mass and the Sunday meal. The order boasts, with some justice, that it was never reformed because never deformed. This dictionary records the Carthusians for the one thing they hold that Scripture plainly honours and for the error of making it a rule of life. Solitary prayer is commanded and exemplified, “when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6), and the Lord himself sought it, “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place” (Mar 1:35). But he sought it and returned. Scripture never makes withdrawal permanent, because it also forbids forsaking the assembly, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25), and the first Christians did the opposite of a cell, “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship” (Act 2:42).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a Carthusian as a monk of the order founded by Bruno, remarkable for austerity; a cell as a small close apartment of a monk; solitude as a lonely life; silence as forbearance of speech; and a recluse as one shut up from the world.

expand to see more

CARTHUSIAN, n. One of an order of monks, so called from Chartreux, the place of their institution by Bruno, remarkable for their austerity.

CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison; also, a small cave or hollow place; the cave or hut of a hermit.

SOLITUDE, n. Loneliness; a state of being alone; a lonely life; forbearance of company.

SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech.

RECLUSE, adj. Shut up; sequestered; retired from the world or from public notice; solitary.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:6 — "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly."

Mar 1:35 — "And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed."

Heb 10:25 — "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching."

Act 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Modern Corruption

The eremitical order of the Grande Chartreuse, 1084: solitary prayer kept with unmatched rigour, and made permanent where Scripture makes it occasional.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that silence and solitude are instruments, not vocations. Scripture sets them in a rhythm with the assembly rather than against it: the Lord withdrew, “And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16), and then came back to the crowds and the twelve. The closet is a place to go, not a place to live.

The live temptation the Carthusian cell represents is the quiet conviction that holiness grows in proportion to distance from other people. The New Testament arranges sanctification the other way, in company that files off the edges, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17), and it treats absenting oneself from the gathering as a danger rather than an advance, “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25). A man may be very alone and very unsanctified.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek tameion (G5009), an inner chamber; Greek eremos (G2048), a desert place; Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together; Greek koinonia (G2842), fellowship; Greek proskartereo (G4342), to continue stedfastly.

expand to see more

Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner storeroom, the closet with a door; “enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door”, Matthew 6:6.

Greek eremos (G2048) — a desert, a solitary place; “departed into a solitary place, and there prayed”, Mark 1:35.

Greek episunagoge (G1997) — the gathering of the assembly; “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together”, Hebrews 10:25.

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, common life; “the apostles' doctrine and fellowship”, Acts 2:42.

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to persist, to continue stedfastly; “they continued stedfastly”, Acts 2:42.

Usage

"“enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6) — the cell's warrant, and its limit."

"“And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16) — withdrawal as rhythm, not residence."

"“Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together” (Heb 10:25) — the command a permanent cell cannot keep."
